The spotted salamander Ambystoma maculatum displays a life history strategy typical of many pond-breeding ambystomatids. The earliest embryonic and larval stages are profoundly influenced by temperature, with eggs that are incubated at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] hatching after approximately 38.5 days [ab = approximately 38.5 days]. This incubation period falls within the broader range of 4 to 7 weeks generally reported for the species, though cooler conditions can extend development considerably. Upon eclosion, the newly emerged aquatic larva carries a modest wet weight at birth of 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of roughly 2 millimeters. These endotrophic larvae initially rely on residual yolk reserves, but they quickly transition to exogenous feeding as they commence active foraging within the vernal pool environment. The timing of subsequent developmental milestones is similarly temperature-dependent, and the larval period under these cool conditions provides the foundation for the growth that will eventually lead to metamorphosis.

Following the hatching event, larvae progress through a period of rapid growth and morphological differentiation within their aquatic habitat. At a constant water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the interval from hatching to the completion of metamorphosis is approximately 150 days after hatching . This duration, which corresponds to roughly 2 to 4 months under natural temperature regimes, encompasses the full array of larval development including limb bud formation, gill resorption, and tail resorption that characterize the metamorphic climax. During this phase, larvae increase dramatically in size and complexity, transitioning from gill-breathing, exogenously feeding tadpoles into post-metamorphic juveniles. The temperature cue is critical, as the rate of development slows markedly in cooler conditions. Once metamorphosis is complete, the terrestrial juveniles emerge from the pond, bearing a snout–vent length at metamorphosis of 1.9 centimeters , a body size that must fuel their subsequent growth through the sub-adult stage.

The post-metamorphic phase is characterized by continued somatic growth and the eventual attainment of sexual maturity. Among females, the time from birth to puberty at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] is approximately 3 years after birth [tp = approximately 3 years after birth], whereas males mature more rapidly, reaching sexual maturity in approximately 2 years after birth [tp = approximately 2 years after birth] under identical thermal conditions. During this prolonged juvenile period, individuals must accumulate sufficient body mass and energy reserves to support future reproductive effort. The pubertal transition is marked by gonad maturation and the onset of gametogenesis, culminating in the first successful breeding season. The size at which females typically achieve puberty reflects this investment, with a snout–vent length at puberty of 6.2 centimeters [Lp = 6.2 centimeters] being a reliable indicator of reproductive competence. This size threshold is notably larger than the size at metamorphosis, underscoring the substantial terrestrial growth phase required before reproductive activation can proceed.

Reproductive adults exhibit a relatively low annual fecundity compared to many other amphibians, consistent with a more K-selected life history. Females produce approximately 100 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 100 eggs per clutch], and they typically deposit a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] when maintained at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This reproductive output results in a modest annual fecundity that is matched by relatively slow growth and late maturation. The gelatinous egg masses are attached to submerged vegetation in vernal pools, where the developing embryos are vulnerable to predation and desiccation. Mature females in this population reach an ultimate wet weight of 12.84 grams [Wwi = 12.84 grams], a body mass that supports the production of these sizable egg clutches. The maximum recorded snout–vent length for adults is 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], although total length, including the tail, can span from 15 to 25 centimeters based on regional field surveys.

Longevity in the spotted salamander is constrained by both environmental and intrinsic physiological factors. The maximum lifespan recorded in wild populations at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] is approximately 32 years [am = approximately 32 years], a remarkably long duration for a temperate-zone amphibian of this body size. This extended lifespan is thought to be associated with its relatively low metabolic rate and the slow pace of life history events, from protracted larval development to delayed reproduction. The attainment of such advanced ages requires repeated successful breeding events across many seasons, as well as the ability to avoid terrestrial predators during the annual migrations to breeding ponds. The species thus exemplifies a slow life history strategy in which high adult survival compensates for relatively low annual reproductive output. The combination of a long juvenile period, modest clutch sizes, and exceptional longevity makes Ambystoma maculatum a compelling subject for studies of life history evolution among pond-breeding urodeles.
